## The Biostatistician Unit of Production

<!-- TODO: workflow diagram -->

| Study | Analysis Report | Manuscript |
|---|---|---|
| Research questions | Data ingestion | Introduction |
| Statistical approaches | Model building | Methods |
| SAS or R jobs | Tables & figures | Results |
| | | Discussion |

Biostats assemble 1+ analysis **jobs** into a single **Analysis Report** built around the researcher's hypothesis.

Researchers synthesize one or more Analysis Reports into a manuscript.

The **Discussion** is a collaboration between PI, researcher, and biostatistician.

## The CORR Origin Story

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### 1997 CORR

-   SAS shop
-   One analyst owns a job
-   Naming conventions and folder structure
-   A social contract — loosely enforced
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Today

-   R and SAS hybrid
-   Team grows to 19 (and more)
-   Conventions extend to R
-   [Discipline doesn't scale under production pressure]{style="color: #C0392B; font-weight: bold;"}
:::
:::::

. . .

`randomForestSRC` was developed here — in CORR. Running it required R.

`ggplot2` outperformed SAS for visualization — so `ggRandomForests` was built to connect them. It was the **13th `ggplot2` extension on CRAN**.

**Nobody planned a hybrid shop. The science pulled R in.**

::: notes
The challenge isn't R vs. SAS. It's that R entered without the infrastructure SAS had. randomForestSRC was developed by Ishwaran and Kogalur in CORR — I wrote ggRandomForests to visualize it. Those two things pulled R into an enterprise SAS shop organically. Not replacing SAS — the science requires both.
:::

## Three steps to production reliability {background-color="#006B5E"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.8em; line-height: 1.8;"}
1. Data ingestion
2. Model building
3. Explainability
:::

# Step 1: Data Ingestion {background-color="#34495e"}

## How it was

Standard study folder structure — always in place. Within `datasets/`, versions accumulate:

-   `cohort_final.sas7bdat`
-   `cohort_final2.sas7bdat`
-   `cohort_final_USE_THIS.sas7bdat`

Version tracking: **filenaming + the OS modified date.**

. . .

**Naming is a social contract** — loosely enforced, inconsistent under pressure.

**Modified dates are fragile** — they reset silently on copy, sync, or backup.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.3em;"}
*Is this the right data? Has it changed?*
:::

::: notes
The folder structure isn't the problem — it works. The problem is what happens inside datasets/ when an extract gets updated. Naming and modified dates weren't designed for this job.
:::

## How we're addressing it [Aspirational]{.badge-aspire}

**Layer governance on top of the structure we already have.**

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What we have

```
study_root/
  analyses/
  datasets/      ← the problem is here
  descriptive/
  distributions/
  documents/
  estimates/
  graphs/
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### What we're adding

-   Dataset manifests: what data, what date, what source
-   Checksums — detect silent changes independent of OS metadata
-   Version in the filename; never overwrite
-   Audit trail: which manifest did this analysis use?
:::
:::::

::: notes
The folder structure is already there and it works. The gap is inside datasets/ — we need a way to know whether the file the analysis ran against is the same file that's there now. Manifests and checksums do that without changing the structure anyone is used to.
:::

## Manifest + checksum in practice [Aspirational]{.badge-aspire}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
**`datasets/built260430.manifest.yml`**

```yaml
dataset:      built260430.sas7bdat
source:       Cardiopulse / STS registry v2.1
pulled_by:    data_manager
pull_date:    2026-04-30
sha256:       a3f8c2d1e4b7f093...
observations: 12847
variables:    428
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Generate on ingest**

```r
digest::digest(
  "datasets/built260430.sas7bdat",
  algo = "sha256", file = TRUE)
```

**Verify before analysis**

```r
stored  <- yaml::read_yaml(
  "datasets/built260430.manifest.yml")$sha256
current <- digest::digest(
  "datasets/built260430.sas7bdat",
  algo = "sha256", file = TRUE)
stopifnot(current == stored)
```

[Filename says *when*. Checksum says *whether*.]{.muted}
:::
::::::

::: notes
The date-stamped filename tells you when the extract was pulled. The checksum independently verifies the file hasn't been modified — a sync, a backup restore, or an accidental overwrite won't change the name but will break the checksum. These two together answer the question: is this the exact file the analysis ran against?
:::

# Step 2: Model Building {background-color="#34495e"}

## How it was

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Analysis jobs**

-   One analyst owns the analysis
-   Copy-paste from previous jobs
-   Runs fine — on that machine, today
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Six months later**

-   R package versions change
-   Results don't match — or the job won't run
-   Serialized models in `estimates/` **fail to load**
-   Nobody knows why
:::
:::::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.4em; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
*Can someone pick up this analysis — even me, in 6 months?*
:::

::: notes
This is what I mean by "works on my machine." The environment wasn't captured — reproduction required the same machine, the same analyst, and a lot of luck.
:::

## Challenge 1: The environment {background-color="#006B5E"}

**How it was:** Packages installed globally — no version pinning, no isolation.

**The problem:**

- Package versions change → results differ, or the job won't run
- Nobody captured the environment, so nobody can reconstruct it
- Serialized models cached in `estimates/` **fail to load** — built against a version that no longer exists

::: notes
Three challenges: the environment, template jobs, standard job flow. Starting with the environment.
:::

## R: `renv` [In use]{.badge-inuse}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
-   Lockfile **records** R version + exact package library
-   Warns on version mismatch; `rv` enforces on private workstations
-   Another biostatistician restores and runs — without version anxiety
-   **The job belongs to the team, not the analyst**
:::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-tip
We run on **RStudio Pro Server** — shared drive, consistent R version. `renv` manages packages and records the R version.
:::
::::
::::::

::: notes
The key word is "handoff." renv makes the job transferable, not just reproducible on your own machine. The lockfile travels with the project; the library itself gets rebuilt locally on renv::restore(). SAS has no equivalent — that's an open problem we note in the status table.
:::

## `renv` in practice

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**New project — run once**

```r
renv::init()       # isolated library + renv.lock
renv::upgrade()    # update renv itself

renv::install("ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR")
renv::install("tidyverse")

renv::snapshot()   # freeze versions
```

**Commit `renv.lock` — not the `renv/` folder.**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Six months later — any analyst**

```r
# Open the .Rproj, then:
renv::restore()    # rebuild exact library
                   # from renv.lock
```

The lockfile is the recipe. `renv::restore()` rebuilds the library on any machine.
:::
::::::

::: notes
Commit the lockfile, not the library folder — the library can be hundreds of megabytes and is machine-specific.
:::

## Challenge 2: Template jobs

**How it was:**

- Heavily commented template programs in a master `templates/` folder
- New project: templates copied in; analyst edits for their target

**The problem:** Structured copy-paste — every study gets a frozen snapshot.

- Analyst improves a template → not propagated back to master
- Master updated → doesn't reach any existing study
- Six studies, six versions, **none canonical**

::: notes
The templates were the attempt to solve copy-paste — and they fell into the same trap. Templates only work if they're version-controlled and distributed like a package.
:::

## R: internal packages [In development]{.badge-dev}

A package **is** a versioned, distributable template system.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Templates in a folder**

- Frozen at project creation
- Changes don't propagate back
- Updates don't reach existing studies
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Code in a package**

- `renv::update()` → pull the fix into any study
- One canonical version at all times
- Roxygen keeps code and examples together — examples run as tests
:::
:::::

. . .

**The hard problems shift — they don't disappear.** Someone has to own the package, manage contributions, and decide when to cut a release.

::: notes
Packages are better than frozen template folders, but the governance problems shift rather than disappear.
:::

:::

## Challenge 3: Standard job flow

**The problem:** Code and output live separately. Any analyst picking up a job reconstructs intent from raw code — no shared structure, no shared mental model.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**SAS `.lst` file** — already does this

-   Code and output in one place
-   Standard SAS workflow for 30 years
-   Figures are separate files outside the `.lst`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**R: Quarto document** [Aspirational]{.badge-aspire}

-   Same concept — code chunks paired with output
-   Figures inline, versioned, self-contained
-   Standard 4-section template: Data · Methods · Explainability · Results
:::
:::::

::: notes
SAS analysts already understand the .lst workflow — paired code and output. Quarto is the same idea with real figures instead of ASCII, and a standard structure any analyst can navigate.
:::


[SAS analysts already understand this workflow. Quarto is a familiar concept made more powerful.]{.muted}

# Step 3: Results and Figures {background-color="#34495e"}

## How it was

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`plot.sas` macro**

- Extends SAS/GRAPH to publication quality
- True axes — origin crosses at 0,0
- Consistent style enforced by the macro
- Figures are **separate files** — outside the `.lst`, no unified output model
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**`ggplot2`**

- Wins on graph variety and theming
- Integrates with Quarto — code and figures in one document
- Bounding box axes — origin doesn't naturally cross at 0,0
- Figure code, themes, and decorators **copy-pasted** across analyses
- Flexibility without guardrails: every analyst reinvents the wheel
:::
:::::

::: notes
This is not a clean win for ggplot2 — it's a trade-off. plot.sas produces publication-quality output with proper axis crossing at 0,0, which ggplot2 doesn't do naturally. ggplot2 wins on flexibility, graph variety, theming, and Quarto integration. hvtiPlotR exists to recover the consistency we had with plot.sas while keeping the ggplot2 advantages.
:::

## The S3 `plot.` pattern [In use]{.badge-inuse}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Package architecture**

- Data transform function → returns an S3 object
- `print.`, `summary.` methods for inspection
- `plot.` method constructs the base `ggplot2` figure
- Analyst decorates using standard `scale_*` and `annotate_*` functions
- Package examples show exactly which calls meet CORR standards
- Consistent theme targets: manuscript, light/dark PowerPoint, posters
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Transform data → S3 object
obj <- corr_analysis(data)

# Base figure
fig <- plot(obj)

# Decorate to standard
fig +
  scale_x_continuous(...) +
  annotate("text", ...)
```

A new analyst builds figures to standard — the examples show how.
:::
::::::

## Our visualization packages [In development]{.badge-dev}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`ggRandomForests`**

[github.com/ehrlinger/ggRandomForests](https://github.com/ehrlinger/ggRandomForests)

Variable importance, partial depth, minimal depth — all as ggplot2 objects. Built around `randomForestSRC` (developed in CORR).

*GitHub-only — removed from CRAN due to dependency drift.*
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**`hvtiPlotR`**

[github.com/ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR](https://github.com/ehrlinger/hvtiPlotR)

Standardizes survival curves, hazard plots, forest plots — CORR themes by default. Decorator functions bridge `ggplot2` gaps toward `plot.sas` standards.

*These packages evolve with the science — never truly finished.*
:::
:::::

# Where Things Stand {background-color="#34495e"}

## Honestly

|   | Status |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Study folder structure | [Adopted]{.badge-adopted} — R and SAS, long-standing standard |
| RStudio Projects + `renv` | [In use]{.badge-inuse} — rolling out now; "easy" win |
| `ggRandomForests`, `hvtiPlotR` | [In development]{.badge-dev} — in use, developing |
| `hvtiPropensityScore` | [In development]{.badge-dev} — not yet production |
| `temporal_hazard` / `mixhazard` | [In development]{.badge-dev} — not yet production |
| SAS environment documentation | [In development]{.badge-dev} — headers + macro versioning |
| Dataset manifests + checksums | [Aspirational]{.badge-aspire} — R and SAS |
| Template programs (R + SAS) | [Aspirational]{.badge-aspire} — templates exist, not standard |
| Platform-agnostic governance checks | [Aspirational]{.badge-aspire} — currently R-only |

: {tbl-colwidths="[45,55]"}


## The framing shift that mattered {background-color="#34495e"}

::: {style="font-size: 1.8em; line-height: 1.5; margin-bottom: 0.8em;"}
"Reproducibility" → **"Production reliability"**
:::

*"Any biostatistician can pick up and continue any job."*

Same investment. Different language. Different outcome.
